children: By Randall W. Forsyth
The triumph of hope over experience. That would describe the bond market's expectations about future inflation.

Despite the repeated surges in prices in recent years, the market's implicit forecast is for inflation to settle back gently to around the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target. That is contrary to what most consumers think, which is why "affordability" has become the buzzword of the midterm election season.

The bond market expects the consumer price index to increase at an annual rate of about 2.34% over the next 10 years. For the coming five years, it anticipates similar growth of 2.36%. That is remarkably quiescent, especially compared with consumers' expectations, at least over the near term. The New York Fed's latest survey found that consumers anticipated inflation of 3.9% in the next year and 3.3% over the next three years.

Those market expectations are derived by subtracting the yield on five- and 10-year Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, from the nominal yield on the corresponding Treasury notes. The difference — or breakeven rate, in market parlance — is the implicit inflation premium.

What's remarkable, James Grant writes in the current Grant's Interest Rate Observer, is that this expected inflation is well below the average inflation rate of 3.35% seen over the past 10 years. It is also lower than the 2.55% inflation rate recorded over the past 30 years.

The latter span included a period of so-called secular stagnation following the 2008-09 financial crisis, when the Fed struggled to lift inflation to its 2% target. It succeeded all too well after the Covid pandemic, when pedal-to-the metal fiscal and monetary stimulus lifted the CPI past 9% in mid-2022.

But since then, the anticipated inflation represented by TIPS' breakevens has been notably subdued. That is especially remarkable given the events of the past five years that pushed prices higher, including Russia's invasion of and war on Ukraine, the imposition of tariffs and other trade barriers, and the Iran war.

Recent inflation readings don't show much slowing in price growth. September's CPI was 3.7% higher than a year earlier, up from August's year-over-year increase of 3.4%, owing to the jump in fuel prices that is top of consumers' minds. Core CPI, which excludes energy and food costs, was up 2.6% in September from a year ago. Producer prices were up 6.3% from a year ago in the latest month; core PPI was up 5.0% from a year earlier.

The Fed prefers to use the personal consumption expenditures index as its inflation gauge instead of the CPI, which is the basis for TIPS adjustments and the increase in Social Security payments, slated to be 3.6% for 2027. The PCE index is derived from components of CPI and PPI.

Many economists estimate that September's PCE price index will be up 3.6% from a year earlier, with core PCE up 3.2%. These figures would be higher than respective year-over-year readings of 3.4% and 3.0% in August. (September's PCE data will be released on Oct. 29.) Omair Sharif, head of Inflation Insights, writes on X.com that a 3.2% gain in core PCE in September would be the biggest annualized monthly gain since 1992, excepting the Covid-related surge.
"Inflation metrics have been above target since the spring of 2021; that's 51/2 years," Carl Weinberg, head of High Frequency Economics, writes in a client note.
How long must inflation remain above 2% before it is recognized as trending above target over the medium term, instead of returning to that target?, he wonders.

As for the TIPS market's subdued inflation forecasts, there are some technical factors that could explain it. A Fed paper published in 2019 cited the lower liquidity and demand for TIPS versus nominal Treasury notes, the world's most traded security. That would tend to raise TIPS yields and thus reduce the difference in yields relative to nominal Treasuries.

Fed officials like to think their stated commitment to bring inflation back to 2% has kept inflation expectations anchored. But a recent paper by Ulrike Malmendier of the University of California, Berkeley, and Stefan Nagel of the University of Chicago's Booth School of Business said future inflation expectations reflect individuals' experiences. Except for the post-Covid spike, most people had become accustomed to the previous low inflation. The Fed can only maintain its credibility by producing results, the authors wrote.

Similarly, governments tend to take positive shocks as permanent and negative ones as transitory, BofA Securities economists Claudio Irigoyen and Antonio Gabriel wrote in a research note. Indeed, the T word has been applied to the succession of supposedly one-off events that pushed up prices, from the supply-chain disruptions following the pandemic to the tariffs imposed by the U.S., countermeasures enacted by trading partners, and the energy spikes related to the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars.

Those of a certain age recall that the food inflation of the early 1970s was blamed on a failed anchovy harvest in South America, which raised agricultural feed costs. Actually, the inflation of that decade was much more fundamental in nature (and once again had energy at its core). In any case, when these supposedly one-time events keep happening, it also suggests things may have changed from the past era of relatively frictionless trade and mostly contained geopolitical conflicts.

As for economic fundamentals, Piper Sandler's economists, led by Nancy Lazar, write that inflation remains sticky at well above 2% because Fed policy is accommodative. Its federal-funds target rate is below 4%, with only a 27% chance of quarter-point hike at its meeting ending Oct. 28, according to CME FedWatch, while nominal gross domestic product is growing by more than 6% year over year.
What they do, not what they say, is what counts.
